title: 22. Interview: Design Swiggy
summary: Interview Q&A for Design Swiggy — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Design Swiggy interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Step 6: Trade-offs & Interview Q&A (5 min)
sections.body:
### Trade-offs Discussed
- **Auto-assignment vs. rider-pickup**: auto-assign is faster (no 30-s decision window) and avoids races, but reduces rider autonomy. Swiggy uses auto-assign because throughput matters at peak; riders can request unassignment with reasons (e.g. vehicle breakdown). Trade-off: throughput > rider flexibility.
- **Batched dispatch vs. single-order**: batching saves ~15% rider-miles but adds 5–8 min to the second order's ETA. Cap = 3 orders/rider; batchable only if pickup < 1.5 km apart and drop direction aligns. Trade-off: cost vs. user-perceived speed.
- **Cassandra LWT vs. Redis lock for state machine**: LWT gives linearisable transitions but ~30 ms p99; Redis lock is faster but needs careful TTL & fencing tokens. We use LWT for the order state machine and Redis SETNX for short-lived rider-busy locks.
- **Cloud-kitchen weighted fair queueing vs. strict FIFO**: FIFO is simple but starves high-value orders during peak; WFQ adds complexity but improves revenue. We use WFQ with priority 1/2/3 lanes.
- **Push vs. WebSocket for order updates**: push for state transitions (reliable across app kills); WebSocket for live rider tracking (sub-second). Use both — push as fallback if WS closed.

### Conceptual Interview Questions

### Q1. How does Swiggy's auto-assignment differ from Uber-style dispatch?
**Answer:** Uber asks one driver at a time and waits for explicit accept/reject (driver-pickup model). Swiggy's Dispatch 2.0 uses **auto-assignment**: the system picks the best rider based on (ETA, on-time %, idle time, batch compatibility) and **assigns** — the rider gets a 15-second window to acknowledge (not accept). If they don't ack, the system moves to the next candidate. The rider cannot reject; they can only request unassignment for documented reasons (vehicle breakdown, address unreachable). The rationale: at India's dinner peak (7–9 PM), throughput is critical — a 30-s driver-decision window per ride is unaffordable. Auto-assignment also enables **batched dispatch** (one rider, up to 3 orders), which Uber's rider-pickup model doesn't easily allow. The trade-off is reduced rider autonomy; Swiggy compensates with earnings guarantees and an unassignment workflow. Auto-assignment is now standard across Indian food-delivery players (Swiggy, Zomato) and ride-hailing (Ola, inDriver hybrid).
**Visual:**
```
Uber-style:        offer rider1 -> wait 15s -> accept/reject -> next
Swiggy Dispatch2:  assign rider1 (best score) -> 15s ack -> if no ack, next
                                   |
                                   v
                            no "reject" option; only "request unassign" (with reason)
```

### Q2. How does batched dispatch work without delaying orders unacceptably?
**Answer:** Batching is conditional — only triggered when (1) a rider already has 1–2 active pickups, (2) the new pickup is within 1.5 km of an existing pickup, and (3) the drop-off directions roughly align (computed via routing-graph ETA, not just haversine). The cap is 3 orders/rider. When dispatch scores candidates, it adds a `load_penalty = 0.3 * active_orders` to the ETA score, so an empty rider is preferred over a loaded one unless the loaded rider is much closer. The second order's ETA is communicated honestly to the user — "rider has 1 pickup before yours, ETA 35 min". The user can opt out by choosing "Express delivery" (a surcharge for single-order). Batching saves Swiggy ~15% rider-miles and ~10% cost per order. The risk is that if the first pickup is delayed (restaurant slow), the second order suffers — mitigated by ETA service continuously recomputing and notifying both users. Batching is disabled during rain/surge when rider supply is tight and per-order ETA matters most.
**Visual:**
```
rider has order A (pickup1, drop1)
new order B comes in
   |
   v
+-----------------------+
| pickup2 within 1.5km?|
| drop2 aligns w/ drop1?|
| rider load < 3?       |
+-----------+-----------+
            |
       yes  |   no -> single-order dispatch for B
            v
assign B to same rider, ETA includes both pickups
```

### Q3. How is surge delivery fee computed and capped?
**Answer:** Surge service consumes `order-placed` (demand) and `rider-online` (supply) Kafka streams over a 5-minute sliding window per H3 hexagon (level 8, ~0.7 km²). `demand = orders_in_window`, `supply = avg_online_riders`. Multiplier `M = clamp(1.0 + 0.5 * log2(demand/supply), 1.0, 2.5)` if demand > supply, else 1.0. To prevent thrash, the per-minute delta is capped at ±0.2× and hysteresis requires a 0.1× change to publish. Swiggy One members get surge waived (the membership service flags the order; pricing service skips the multiplier). Surge is recomputed every minute but only published when changed meaningfully. There's also a **hard cap** of 2.5× enforced by the pricing service regardless of cache value — a circuit breaker against runaway surges during incidents. Surge revenue is shared with the rider (a portion goes to the rider's earnings, incentivising them to log in during peak). Surge is shown transparently to the user at checkout with the multiplier visible.
**Visual:**
```
demand / supply per H3 cell
        |
        v
M = clamp(1 + 0.5 * log2(d/s), 1.0, 2.5)
        |
        v
delta cap +/- 0.2/min, hysteresis 0.1
        |
        v
Redis surge:{h3} TTL 5min
        |
        v
pricing service: delivery_fee * M (capped at 2.5x)
```

### Q4. How does the cloud-kitchen KDS ensure fairness across brands sharing one kitchen?
**Answer:** A Swiggy Access cloud kitchen hosts 10+ brand menus (e.g. a single kitchen preparing "Burger King", "Subway", "Behrouz Biryani" simultaneously). The KDS service maintains per-station queues — each station (e.g. "grill", "tandoor", "Chinese wok") has its own Redis sorted set. When an order arrives, each item is routed to its station based on `menu_items.station`. Within a station, items are queued with **weighted fair queueing**: priority 1 (normal), 2 (high-value > ₹800 or Swiggy One), 3 (bulk/catering). The score is `enqueue_ts * (1/priority)`, so priority-2 items advance ~2× faster. Each station's display shows the next item to cook. When an item completes (`plated`), it transitions to `ready` and the order-service checks if all items are ready → triggers `ready_for_pickup`. To prevent one brand's burst from starving others, we add a per-brand weight cap: a brand can occupy at most 60% of a station's active queue. The KDS also exposes real-time dashboards to kitchen managers showing queue depth, prep time SLA breaches, and station bottlenecks — enabling dynamic staff reallocation.
**Visual:**
```
order placed at cloud kitchen (10 brands)
        |
        v  split by item.station
+--------+--------+--------+
| grill  | tandoor| wok    |   (per-station Redis sorted sets)
+---+----+---+----+---+----+
    |        |        |
    v        v        v
  WFQ: priority 2 advances 2x faster; per-brand cap 60%
    |
    v  all items ready -> order ready_for_pickup
```

### Q5. How does Swiggy handle the rider location write fan-in (50 K pings/s)?
**Answer:** Three layers. (1) **Client-side batching**: the rider app batches pings every 5 s and sends them in a single HTTPS request (5 pings per request) — reduces request count 5×. (2) **Ingestion service with pipelined Redis writes**: the ingestion service receives pings, validates, and writes to Redis GEO via pipelined `GEOADD` (batches of 100 commands per pipeline round-trip). Redis Cluster with 16 shards distributes riders by `hash(rider_id)`. (3) **Kafka spout for durability**: every ping is also published to Kafka `rider-location` (partitioned by rider_id) — if Redis is lost, we can rebuild the GEO index from Kafka. Read path: `GEORADIUS` is O(log N + M); a 2.5 km scan in a dense city returns ~50 candidates in ~5 ms. Cross-shard queries are rare because riders in one H3 cell map to one shard via consistent hashing on the cell ID. The system sustains 50 K pings/s at < 30% CPU on a 16-shard Redis Cluster. P99 write latency < 5 ms; p99 read latency < 10 ms.
**Visual:**
```
rider app (batch 5 pings/req) -> ingestion svc
        |
        v
+-------------------+        +-------------------+
| Kafka rider-loc   | -----> | consumer pipeline |
+-------------------+        | (batches of 100)  |
                             +---------+---------+
                                       |
                                       v
                             Redis Cluster (16 shards)
                             GEOADD per shard ~5ms p99
                                       |
                                       v
                             GEORADIUS queries ~5-10ms
```

### Q6. How does Swiggy's Instamart achieve 10-minute delivery?
**Answer:** Instamart is structurally different from food delivery. (1) **Dark stores**: pre-positioned inventory at ~500 dark stores nationwide, each ~1 500–3 000 SKUs, located in dense neighborhoods. (2) **Pre-assigned riders**: each dark store has a pool of 8–15 riders physically present at the store; no dispatch needed — the rider is already there. (3) **Picking within 2 min**: order is sent to the store's pick-and-pack system (mobile app guiding the picker through aisles); items are picked and bagged in < 2 min. (4) **Routing**: drop-off is within 1.5 km; rider travel is 5–7 min. (5) **No restaurant dependency**: the bottleneck is picking, not cooking — predictable. Total: place → pick (2 min) → travel (6 min) → deliver = ~10 min. The architecture simplifies: no `restaurant_accepted` state, no auto-assignment; the order is assigned to the next available in-store rider. Inventory is synced to the menu service in real-time — if an item's stock drops below threshold, it's marked out-of-stock on the app within 30 s. The trade-off: limited catalog (~2 000 SKUs vs. restaurants' 50-item menus) and high fixed cost (dark store rent).
**Visual:**
```
user places Instamart order
        |
        v
dark store picks (2 min)  <-- picker with mobile app
        |
        v
in-store rider pool (8-15 riders always present)
        |
        v
travel 1.5km (5-7 min)  <-- no dispatch needed
        |
        v
deliver (~10 min total)
```

### Q7. How does Swiggy ensure order state machine integrity across microservices?
**Answer:** The order service is the **single source of truth** for the order state machine. State transitions are persisted in Cassandra using **Lightweight Transactions (LWT)** — `UPDATE orders SET status = ? WHERE order_id = ? IF status = ?`. This ensures linearisable compare-and-set: if two services try to transition `preparing → ready_for_pickup` simultaneously, only one succeeds (`applied=true`); the other gets `applied=false` and must re-read. The valid transitions are enforced in code (`VALID_TRANSITIONS` map). Other services (dispatch, payment, KDS) consume `order-events` from Kafka and react — but they cannot modify the state directly; they call the order service's transition API. The latest state is cached in Redis (`order:{id}:status` TTL 1 h, invalidated on transition) for fast reads by the user/restaurant apps. For multi-region active-active, Cassandra LWT is pinned to a quorum in the order's home DC (determined by `city_id`), avoiding cross-DC latency. The combination of LWT (correctness) + Redis cache (read latency) + Kafka events (decoupled reactions) is the standard pattern for stateful microservices.
**Visual:**
```
dispatch svc  ---POST /orders/{id}/transition--->  order svc
                                                        |
KDS svc      ---POST /orders/{id}/transition--->       |
                                                        v
                                            Cassandra LWT:
                                            UPDATE ... IF status = ?
                                                        |
                                       applied=true? --> publish order-events
                                                        |
                                                        v
                                            Redis order:{id}:status invalidated
```

### Scenario-Based Interview Questions

### Q1. During the IPL final, dinner orders spike 4× in Mumbai. Dispatch is failing — riders are rejecting/unassigning, orders auto-cancelling after 8 min. How do you stabilise?
**Answer:** Triage: this is a demand-supply mismatch with secondary rider churn (frustrated riders logging off). Immediate actions: (1) **Throttle demand** — surge to 2.0× (cap), show "high demand, longer wait" warnings at checkout, hide restaurants with ETA > 75 min from discovery. (2) **Recall riders** — push "IPL bonus hour: earn ₹300 extra" to recently-offline riders in Mumbai; offer login bonus. (3) **Disable batching** — in supply-crisis mode, batching actually slows the second order; switch to single-order dispatch so each order gets dedicated rider attention. (4) **Widen dispatch radius** — from 2.5 km to 4 km (accept slightly higher pickup time). (5) **Auto-accept restaurants** — force auto-accept for opted-in chains to remove the 90-s restaurant SLA bottleneck. (6) **Prioritise Swiggy One members** — non-members see "currently unavailable in your area"; members get priority dispatch. (7) **Communicate transparently** — push "your order may take 60 min due to high demand" so users don't cancel. Medium-term: pre-position riders using IPL-aware demand forecasting (predict 3× spike 30 min before match start). Long-term: increase Mumbai rider base target for IPL season. Post-incident: review rider churn rate during the spike — if > 15% logged off, the issue is rider morale, not just supply.
**Visual:**
```
4x demand spike
        |
        v
+--------------------+   +---------------------+   +-------------------+
| surge 2.0x (cap)   |   | recall offline riders|  | disable batching  |
+--------------------+   +---------------------+   +-------------------+
        |
        v
+--------------------+   +---------------------+
| widen radius 4km   |   | auto-accept chains  |
+--------------------+   +---------------------+
        |
        v
hide ETA>75min, prioritise Swiggy One, transparent comms
```

### Q2. A user reports they received the wrong order. The rider delivered a sealed bag from restaurant A but the user ordered from restaurant B. How does the system prevent and investigate this?
**Answer:** Prevention safeguards: (1) **Restaurant-side bag label** — each order has a QR code printed on the seal; the rider app scans the QR at pickup (`picked_up` transition requires scan). The QR encodes `order_id`; mismatch with the assigned order blocks the transition. (2) **Geofence at pickup** — rider must be within 50 m of the restaurant's pinned location to scan. (3) **OTP at delivery** for orders > ₹500 — rider enters the OTP shown in the user's app. (4) **Bag seal photo** — rider uploads a photo of the sealed bag at pickup (CV model checks the seal is intact). Investigation steps: pull the order's event timeline from Kafka — was the QR scan recorded? Was the rider at the right restaurant (geofence)? Did the rider have multiple pickups (batched) and mix them up? Was the OTP entered? If the QR scan was skipped or overridden (operator override), that's the root cause — flag the override workflow. Resolution: refund the user, debit the rider if negligent, rerun the order for free. Post-mortem: if QR scan was bypassed, tighten the override policy. If restaurant labelled the bag wrong, add a restaurant-side checklist requirement. Pattern of mix-ups → rider retraining.
**Visual:**
```
rider at restaurant
        |
        v
+--------------------------+
| scan QR on bag seal      |  mismatch? -> REJECT pickup
+--------------------------+
        |
        v
+--------------------------+
| geofence check (<50m)    |  outside? -> REJECT
+--------------------------+
        |
        v
+--------------------------+
| OTP at delivery (>Rs500) |  wrong? -> REJECT delivery
+--------------------------+
        |
        v
delivered -> user reports wrong order
        |
        v
investigate: QR scan log + geofence + OTP + bag photo
```

### Q3. A cloud kitchen's grill station queue grows to 40 items while the tandoor station is idle. The kitchen manager wants to rebalance. How does the KDS support this?
**Answer:** The KDS exposes a real-time dashboard (per-station queue depth, prep time SLA, station idle time). When the grill queue breaches threshold (> 20 items for 5 min), an alert fires. The kitchen manager opens the KDS tablet's "Rebalance" view: it shows staff allocations and suggests moving one cook from tandoor to grill. The KDS supports **item rerouting** — items that can be cooked on either station (e.g. a paneer tikka can go to grill or tandoor) are flagged with `flexible_station = true`. The manager clicks "Reroute flexible items to tandoor" — the KDS moves those items from `kds:{kitchen_id}:queue:grill` to `kds:{kitchen_id}:queue:tandoor` atomically (Redis transaction). The station displays update within 1 s. For items that are grill-only, the manager can mark them as "delayed" and notify affected users (ETA recomputed + 10 min). Longer-term, the KDS analytics recommend staff allocation patterns based on historical demand by hour and day. The dashboard also shows per-station throughput (items/min) so the manager can identify bottlenecks. This is essentially a real-time operations console layered on the KDS Redis data structures.
**Visual:**
```
grill queue: 40 items (breach!)   tandoor queue: 3 items (idle)
        |                                |
        v                                v
+----------------------------------------------+
| KDS dashboard alerts manager                 |
| suggests: reroute flexible items to tandoor |
+----------------------+-----------------------+
                       |
                       v
            Redis transaction:
            ZMOVE grill -> tandoor (flexible items)
                       |
                       v
            station displays refresh in 1s
            ETA recomputed for affected orders
```

### Q4. The Redis GEO cluster hosting rider positions goes down entirely. Dispatch can't query riders. What's the degraded-mode behaviour?
**Answer:** This is a P0 incident. Degraded mode: (1) **Fallback to Elasticsearch `geo_distance`**: the geolocation service has a secondary index of rider positions in Elasticsearch (updated by the same Kafka `rider-location` stream, with 10 s lag). Dispatch queries ES instead — slower (~50 ms vs 5 ms) but functional. (2) **Reduce dispatch throughput**: cap assignments to 50/s (vs 120/s normal) to protect ES; queue excess orders with a 30-s delay. (3) **Broadcast fallback**: for high-value orders, broadcast to all riders within 5 km via push ("Earn ₹X bonus") — first-come-first-served via Redis SETNX (using a different Redis cluster, e.g. the surge-cache cluster repurposed). (4) **User communication**: show "live tracking temporarily degraded" in the app; fall back to coarse ETA based on `placed_at + historical prep + travel`. (5) **Recovery**: bring up Redis Cluster from snapshot (RPO ~1 min) + replay Kafka `rider-location` from the last offset to rebuild the GEO index. Estimated recovery: 10–15 min. Post-incident: validate the ES fallback path is always in sync (it should be — both consume the same Kafka topic). Add a chaos test for Redis GEO outage in staging. Root-cause the Redis failure (likely a single-shard hot spot or a config push).
**Visual:**
```
Redis GEO cluster DOWN (P0)
        |
        v
+-----------------------------+
| fallback to Elasticsearch   |
| geo_distance (50ms, 10s lag)|
+-------------+---------------+
              |
              v
+-----------------------------+
| throttle dispatch 50/s      |
| broadcast fallback for high-value
+-------------+---------------+
              |
              v
+-----------------------------+
| user app: "tracking degraded"|
| coarse ETA from placed_at    |
+-----------------------------+
              |
              v
recover: Redis from snapshot + Kafka replay (10-15 min)
```

### Q5. A restaurant partner reports their orders are being auto-cancelled despite them accepting within 30 s. Investigation shows the accept API call from their tablet is timing out. How do you fix this?
**Answer:** Diagnosis: the partner app's `POST /restaurants/{id}/orders/{order_id}/accept` call is timing out at the network layer (poor restaurant Wi-Fi, intermittent 4G). The 90-s SLA timer fires before the accept reaches the server. Fixes: (1) **Idempotent accept with retry** — partner app retries the accept call with the same idempotency key; server deduplicates. (2) **Offline queue** — partner app queues the accept locally if network is down; syncs when network returns. The order service accepts late arrivals if the SLA timer hasn't fired; if it has, the order is already cancelled — show a clear message to the partner. (3) **Extend SLA for low-bandwidth restaurants** — detect slow networks (accept call > 5 s) and bump SLA to 120 s for that restaurant. (4) **Accept via SMS/IVR fallback** — send an IVR call to the restaurant's primary phone at 60 s: "Order #{id} waiting, press 1 to accept". The IVR channel doesn't depend on the tablet. (5) **Auto-accept opt-in** — encourage restaurants to enable auto-accept for orders below a threshold (saves the SLA dance entirely). (6) **Health monitoring** — restaurant service tracks per-restaurant accept latency; if a restaurant's p99 > 10 s, flag for partner-ops follow-up (tablet replacement, Wi-Fi setup help). Post-incident: add a "network health" indicator on the partner app dashboard so restaurants can self-diagnose.
**Visual:**
```
partner app --(accept, network slow)--> timeout
        |
        v
+-----------------------------+
| idempotent retry w/ same key|
| offline queue if no network |
+-------------+---------------+
              |
              v
+-----------------------------+
| IVR fallback at 60s         |
| "press 1 to accept"         |
+-------------+---------------+
              |
              v
+-----------------------------+
| auto-accept opt-in for < Rs500 orders
+-----------------------------+
```

### Q6. Swiggy One subscribers complain they're seeing surge fees despite the "free delivery + no surge" promise. Investigation shows the surge-waiver logic in the pricing service has a bug. How do you design surge-waiver correctly?
**Answer:** The bug is likely a coupling issue — the surge-waiver check is in the pricing service but depends on membership state that may be stale. Correct design: (1) **Membership state at order placement** — the order service fetches the user's Swiggy One membership status (`GET /users/{id}/membership`) at order placement and stamps it on the order (`is_swiggy_one: true`). This becomes the canonical flag for the order's lifetime — even if the membership expires mid-order, the original flag applies. (2) **Pricing service reads the stamped flag** — `if order.is_swiggy_one: surge_mult = 1.0`. No dependency on a live membership lookup. (3) **Display surge transparently** — even with waiver, show the user "Surge 1.8x (waived for Swiggy One)" so they perceive value. (4) **Audit trail** — log the surge computation: `(base_fee, surge_mult, is_swiggy_one, final_fee)`. If a One member is charged surge, the audit trail shows the bug location. (5) **Reconciliation job** — nightly scan: for every One-member order, verify `final_fee == base_fee` (no surge). Mismatches trigger auto-refund + alert. (6) **Feature flag** — surge-waiver logic behind a flag so it can be disabled during incidents without a deploy. (7) **Test coverage** — add integration tests covering: One member during surge, non-member during surge, One member during no-surge, membership-expired-mid-order. The root cause of the original bug is likely that the pricing service was querying membership live and hit a cache-miss-stale scenario; stamping at order placement eliminates this class of bug.
**Visual:**
```
order placement:
   order svc fetches membership, stamps is_swiggy_one on order
        |
        v
pricing service reads stamped flag:
   if is_swiggy_one: surge_mult = 1.0  (display "waived")
        |
        v
audit log: (base, surge_mult, is_one, final)
        |
        v
nightly reconciliation: One-member order final==base? -> refund if not
```

### Q7. Swiggy wants to expand Instamart to a new city with 10 dark stores. How does the architecture handle the launch?
**Answer:** Instamart's architecture is simpler than restaurant delivery — no dispatch, no restaurant-accept state. Launch steps: (1) **Dark store setup** — each store gets a tablet with the Instamart Store App (pick-and-pack UI, inventory management). Inventory is loaded into MySQL `menu_items` with `is_instamart = true` and a `dark_store_id`. (2) **Rider pool** — recruit ~10–15 riders per dark store; they're pre-assigned to the store zone in Redis `riders:instamart:{store_id}` (not the city-wide GEO index). (3) **Catalog sync** — the new city's catalog is added to Elasticsearch `restaurants` index with `is_instamart = true`; discovery service returns Instamart cards for users within 1.5 km of a dark store (geofence). (4) **Order flow** — order placed → order service detects `is_instamart` → bypasses restaurant-accept state → directly routes to the dark store's pick-and-pack queue → in-store rider picks → delivers. (5) **No dispatch needed** — the order is assigned to the next available in-store rider via a simple Redis queue (`instamart:{store_id}:riders`); FIFO. (6) **Inventory real-time** — picker scans items at pick time; stock decrements; if stock drops below threshold, the item is marked out-of-stock on the app within 30 s. (7) **Monitoring** — per-store dashboards: orders/hr, pick time p99, rider idle time, stock-out rate. (8) **Cost**: ~₹3–5 L/month per dark store (rent + staff + riders); break-even at ~600 orders/day. The architecture scales linearly — adding a city is mostly an ops exercise (store setup, rider recruitment, catalog ingestion).
**Visual:**
```
new city launch (10 dark stores)
        |
        v
+-----------------------------+
| each store: tablet + inventory in MySQL
| riders pre-assigned to store zone
+-------------+---------------+
              |
              v
+-----------------------------+
| catalog in Elasticsearch    |
| is_instamart=true, geofence 1.5km
+-------------+---------------+
              |
              v
+-----------------------------+
| order flow: no restaurant_accept
| -> pick (2min) -> deliver (6min)
+-----------------------------+
              |
              v
per-store dashboards, ~600 orders/day break-even
```
